prime.problem: Thirteen cards each name a tool: processes, threads, locks, semaphores, monitors, context switches, schedulers, asyncio. Without a map they read as thirteen separate APIs, and you pick one by habit. Pick the wrong unit and you either gain nothing (4 threads on fib(27): 1.00×) or pay a start-up cost bigger than the work (72 ms per fresh process).
prime.fits: This is the course map. It builds on cs-4's back-of-envelope habit (put a number on each term) and ties the five parts together with one question: what is the work waiting on, and how cheaply can you run more of it at once without losing shared data?
expect: CPU-bound vs I/O-bound decides the unit
the cost ladder: 58 ns lock → µs switches → 72 ms process
the cheapest guard that fits: lock, semaphore, condition
prime.goal: Draw the whole course as one causal map from "what is the work waiting on?" to "which unit and which guard", and say which card settles each decision and with which measured number.

attend: In the one-relationship formula, which unit raises p, which raises k, and which one makes n·c the biggest term?
Why does asyncio's 10,000-wait run take 0.25 s instead of the ideal 0.1 s, and what does the leftover say about a task's cost?
The decision table pairs each need with one number. Which rows are about speed, which about correctness, and which about making progress at all?
Why does the overview say correctness "has no bar" in the wrong-choice chart?
Which three conditions does the overview name under which its advice stops applying?

must: Ask what the work waits on → CPU-bound needs more cores running Python at once (raise p) → on a GIL build only processes do that (0.121 → 0.032 s) → on free-threaded 3.14t threads do it too (0.045 → 0.017 s)

I/O-bound work needs more waits in flight (raise k) → threads release the GIL while blocked (8 sleeps: 0.835 → 0.105 s) → but each thread is a kernel object with a stack → for thousands of waits, asyncio tasks on one thread (10,000 in 0.25 s)

Each unit has a price c spanning six orders of magnitude (58 ns lock, ≤ 4–7 µs switch, 72 ms spawn) → a unit costlier than the work it does makes things slower → reuse pools, hold locks briefly, park waits as tasks

Two units touching the same data → read-modify-write races lose updates (100,096 of 400,000 kept) → guard with the cheapest fitting tool → take locks in one global order (no cycle) and back off at random when retrying (no lockstep)
elevated: Switch costs on this course are halved round trips (13.6 µs pipe, 8.2 µs Event) → they are ceilings that include Python's own work → the cold cache and TLB after a switch can cost more than the switch itself
reference: the cost-ladder figure's exact rungs and the log-scale bar rule
per-card headline numbers in the decision table (671,169 spin checks, 6,143 threads, 4.93 retries…)
the OSTEP chapter list (4–9, 13, 19, 26–33) and the Python doc pages

compress.prompt: Close the page and draw the course's causal map from memory: start at "what does the work wait on?", branch to CPU (processes, or threads without the GIL) and to I/O (threads for dozens, asyncio for thousands), then add a third branch for shared data (lock → semaphore → condition; lock order; backoff) and a fourth for what a switch and a scheduler cost. Hang all 13 cards on it with one number each.
checklist: the formula's three terms: compute ÷ p, waits ÷ k, units × cost
the GIL keeps p = 1 for threads on 3.10; processes or 3.14t raise it
threads for dozens of waits, asyncio for thousands
any shared read-modify-write needs a guard, whatever the unit
deadlock is a cycle (fix: one order); livelock is lockstep (fix: random backoff)
switches cost µs plus cold caches; schedulers trade turnaround against response

retrieve.q: Explain the overview's "in one breath" stance: why ask what the work waits on before choosing processes, threads or asyncio?
answer: the bottleneck decides which term of the formula can shrink: CPU work needs p > 1, waiting needs k > 1
under the GIL, threads keep p at 1, so they help only waits
the wrong unit adds n·c (start-up, stacks, switches) without shrinking the big term

retrieve.q: Walk the formula through 4 × fib(27) on 4 freshly spawned processes, rather than a warm pool. Which term dominates, and what does that tell you to do?
answer: one fresh process costs 72 ms, already more than twice the compute term (60% of the serial job)
so n·c dominates: start the pool once and reuse it, or don't parallelise jobs this small

retrieve.q: Your team must hold 5,000 slow HTTP calls open at once from Python 3.10. Using the overview's table, choose a unit and say what the other two choices would cost.
answer: asyncio: tasks are small heap objects, 10,000 finished in 0.25 s
a thread each runs into the per-process thread cap and a stack per thread (failed at 6,143 on the M3); a pool of 8 threads serialises into rounds
processes add 72 ms each and gain nothing, because the work is waiting, not computing

retrieve.q: The wrong-choice chart's biggest bar is "new process per message → reuse one" (≈ 5,300×). What do that row and "parking waits as tasks" have in common?
answer: both remove n·c: paying for a unit per item instead of reusing a cheap one
72 ms vs 13.6 µs per message; a kernel thread plus stack vs a 1.6 KB task
neither changes the useful work; they stop paying overhead for it

compare.q: cs-5 coordinates replicas across machines; this course coordinates threads inside one. Which problems appear in both, and which design choice makes each cheaper or dearer here?
answer: both have lost updates without coordination, and retries that need backoff (livelock here, retry storms there)
here a lock is 58 ns because threads share memory and an atomic instruction; there agreement costs a network round trip
here a thread that waits is known to be alive; there a timeout can't tell a crash from a slow reply

compare.q: cs-6 is about touching less data; this course is about running work concurrently. Where do they meet, and which course's rule decides each part?
answer: they meet at the cache: a context switch leaves the next task cold caches and TLB (the hardware card), which cs-6's cache-conscious structures try to avoid
cs-6 decides the data layout and access pattern; cs-7 decides how many units touch it and how they share it
both say: overhead you don't need (misses, units, switches) often dwarfs the work

predict.q: You move a CPU-bound Python service from 3.10 to free-threaded 3.14t and switch its ProcessPoolExecutor to a ThreadPoolExecutor. Which of the overview's rules change, and what new bug might appear on the first day? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: The CPU rule flips toward threads: without the GIL, 4 threads on fib(27) gained 2.65× (0.045 → 0.017 s), close to processes' 3.46×, and threads share the heap so nothing is pickled. The new bug: any shared read-modify-write that the GIL happened to protect now loses updates, as plain c["n"] += 1 kept only 1,082,391 of 4,000,000. Every shared mutable value needs a lock, which the processes never needed because they shared nothing.

apply.task: Design review: a Python 3.10 job does three things per batch: (a) 4 CPU-heavy chunks of about 0.03 s each, (b) 2,000 HTTP calls of about 0.1 s each, (c) increments a shared done counter after each item. Pick a unit and a guard for each part, write the formula term that each choice shrinks, and estimate the wall time of (a) and (b) from the course's numbers.
apply.done: You have three rows (part, unit, guard, term shrunk, estimate), and your (a) estimate says whether a fresh pool or a warm one is used and why that changes the answer by 72 ms.
apply.hint: (a) a warm ProcessPoolExecutor(4): 0.121 / 4 ≈ 0.03 s, as measured (0.032 s); a fresh one adds a spawn's 72 ms. (b) asyncio: ideal 0.1 s, and at the measured ≈ 15 µs of overhead per task, 2,000 tasks add about 0.03 s; a pool of 8 threads would take 2,000 / 8 × 0.1 = 25 s. (c) a Lock, or per-worker counters summed at the end; in asyncio a counter with no await between read and write needs no lock.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: that threads win CPU work on 3.14t, or that the GIL was hiding a race?
Can you rebuild the formula's three terms from memory and put a measured number on each?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: bottleneck → unit, or shared data → guard?
Which card's headline number in the decision table could you not rebuild from its mechanism?
Which part of the map will you reopen first the next time you write concurrent code?
